summary: A Leaffin.com article, last updated May 12, 2019, asking whether turtles are a good or bad fit for aquaponics as an alternative to fish. It covers turtle biology (cold-blooded, winter oxygen uptake through throat and cloacal tissues), argues turtle waste is a nutrient source that biofilters can digest, and lists care concerns including Salmonella risk, basking needs, and predation on fish. The author ultimately suggests keeping the system as decoration rather than growing edible plants.
one_line: Leaffin article weighing turtles against fish in aquaponics, covering turtle biology, waste nutrients, and Salmonella and care concerns.
key_facts: The article was last updated on May 12, 2019 and is published on Leaffin.com in the Aquaponics category.
Turtles are cold-blooded (ectotherms), so their body temperature changes with the ambient environment.
Turtles can absorb dissolved oxygen from water through specialized tissues in the throat and just inside the tail opening.
The article states that turtle waste provides nutrients for plants in an aquaponic system.
In an aquaponic system, microbes in a biofilter digest turtle waste, removing the need for carbon sponges or water replacement.
The article lists six reasons to use turtles instead of fish, including that turtles poo more, have more personality, are hardier, and can be kept as pets.
The article identifies Salmonella as the biggest concern for keeping turtles in aquaponics.
The article says Salmonella risk from turtles is usually due to poor care and is not as common as most people think.
Turtles need something to crawl onto so they can rest and bask; otherwise they may grow tired swimming and drown.
The article says omnivorous turtles will eat fish, invertebrates, fruits and seeds, aquatic plants and algae.
The author recommends not growing edible plants in a turtle aquaponic system and keeping the whole system as decoration.
The article advises preventing water from splashing onto vegetables and washing hands and vegetables before handling or eating.
Turtles need strong water flow and filtration and a dynamic habitat to work well in aquaponics.
The article says turtles are easy to market when small but hard to care for properly over the long run, especially as they grow.
